method: Each listed item was read with its stem, all options, keyed answer(s), explanations and takeaway. Statuses are manually reasoned, not inferred from a schema or automated pass rule.
limitations: Independent AI editorial/clinical-reasoning screen; not external clinician validation or psychometric validation.
Pass applies only to the recorded content hash. New or changed content requires further review.
No comparison against proprietary examination items; originality judged from author provenance and item content.
Cross-bank learning-objective overlap remains provisional until all batches are available.
Source checks below support only the explicitly associated claims; other category references are general reading unless specifically verified.

sourceChecks.note: FDA primary guidance retrieved: even small food/sugar residue affects capillary measurements; wash/dry hands.
CBS primary guidance retrieved: surgical bleeding risk rises at low platelets; procedure/context affect thresholds, so review rather than universal transfusion advice is appropriate.
BC emergency guidance retrieved: sodium below 125 with altered mental status is concerning and needs urgent clinical assessment; no correction rate prescribed by item.
BC emergency guidance retrieved: suspected hyperkalaemia includes ECG/monitoring and lab redraw; hemolysis does not license dismissal.
ASPEN position-paper abstract retrieved: albumin/prealbumin reflect inflammation and should not substitute for malnutrition assessment.
Primary sepsis guidance retrieved during legacy review for immediate treatment priority; full culture timing recommendation not separately opened in this batch.

items.assessment: The visibly undersized cuff is a concrete measurement defect in an otherwise comfortable client; correct-size repeat is the best available first step. The item does not say to ignore symptoms or persistent severe values.
Full-minute assessment of an irregular pulse is correct, but skin temperature cannot quantify pulse and is irrelevant filler.
issues: Full-minute assessment of an irregular pulse is correct, but skin temperature cannot quantify pulse and is irrelevant filler.

options: Repeat only after the next scheduled round
Use the automated blood-pressure machine’s displayed pulse rate as the complete rhythm assessment
Count the apical pulse for a full minute
Multiply a ten-second count by six
why: Symptoms and a new irregularity need timely assessment.
An automated displayed rate does not replace assessment of a symptomatic irregular rhythm.
A full assessment better characterizes an irregular rhythm.
A brief sample may misrepresent an irregular rate.

items.assessment: Rate/depth/alertness together assess ventilation more directly than pain relief, a short count or saturation alone. Supplemental oxygen can leave saturation reassuring despite hypoventilation. Clear assessment objective, not a complete emergency-management algorithm.

Recent fruit handling is a specific contamination cue; washed/dried repeat is appropriate for a well client before acting on an unexpected result. Primary FDA advice and fruit-peeling study support this mechanism.
Comparable-weight conditions are sound; disregarding all weights for admission is a conspicuous overreaction.
issues: Comparable-weight conditions are sound; disregarding all weights for admission is a conspicuous overreaction.

options: Average both measurements immediately
Assume fluid overload without assessment
Convert today’s weight by subtracting a standard clothing allowance without reweighing
Repeat under comparable measurement conditions
why: Averaging does not correct incompatible conditions.
Measurement differences may explain some of the apparent change.
An assumed clothing correction does not account for scale differences or actual clothing weight.
Standardization helps distinguish real change from measurement variation.

items.assessment: Output reconciliation is correct, but an independent bolus is a weak out-of-scope distraction.
issues: Output reconciliation is correct, but an independent bolus is a weak out-of-scope distraction.

options: Label the charted absence as oliguria and request treatment before checking the reported voids
Enter estimated volumes from memory
Clarify and assess the missing output
Report confirmed anuria from the chart
why: Assess and reconcile the conflicting information before presenting absent output as confirmed.
Unmeasured voids should not be documented as measured amounts.
Incomplete recording may mimic reduced renal output.
The chart conflicts with reported voiding and needs verification.

items.assessment: Platelets48 before an invasive procedure warrant procedural-team review. The key appropriately escalates rather than prescribing a universal transfusion threshold, which depends on procedure and context.
Symptomatic substantial postoperative haemoglobin fall is important, but iron snack and walking are implausible alternatives.
issues: Symptomatic substantial postoperative haemoglobin fall is important, but iron snack and walking are implausible alternatives.

options: Assess for bleeding and promptly escalate
Attribute the fall to IV-fluid dilution and continue routine observation without assessing symptoms
Repeat the blood sample before checking circulation because a laboratory error is possible
Hold the next anticoagulant dose and wait for the next routine review without contacting the team
why: The symptomatic decline needs evaluation for blood loss.
Dilution can affect the value, but new dizziness with this decline needs assessment for bleeding/perfusion.
Confirmation may be appropriate, but should not delay assessing a symptomatic client.
Medication decisions do not replace prompt evaluation of possible acute bleeding.

items.assessment: Renal trend context is correct but bedtime is unrelated and makes the SATA answer trivial.
issues: Renal trend context is correct but bedtime is unrelated and makes the SATA answer trivial.

options: Recent medicines and contrast exposure
Report only the latest creatinine number without the prior value or collection date
Report only the usual daily fluid prescription without checking actual intake and losses
Recent urine output and fluid balance
why: Potential renal stressors guide further assessment.
The magnitude and timing of change are clinically important.
The intended prescription does not establish the recent fluid balance or urine response.
These help characterize the acute renal change.

items.assessment: Hyponatraemia with confusion warrants urgent assessment; salty food and plain water are weak options that bypass realistic nursing choices.
issues: Hyponatraemia with confusion warrants urgent assessment; salty food and plain water are weak options that bypass realistic nursing choices.

options: Request a repeat sodium before checking neurological status because the first value may be erroneous
Repeat the orientation check after a rest period before reporting the sodium result
Promptly assess neurological status and escalate
Apply a fluid restriction without reporting the new confusion or clarifying the cause
why: Verification must not delay assessment of a symptomatic electrolyte abnormality.
A new neurological change with sodium 122 needs prompt evaluation, not normalization.
Neurological change with marked hyponatraemia needs urgent review.
Treatment depends on clinical cause and symptoms; a unilateral restriction does not replace urgent assessment/escalation.

items.assessment: The stem omits the potassium value, so the urgent/critical framing is imprecise. Supply a clinically important result and avoid next-week/normal-filing caricatures.
issues: The stem omits the potassium value, so the urgent/critical framing is imprecise. Supply a clinically important result and avoid next-week/normal-filing caricatures.

options: Wait for the routine morning laboratory draw because haemolysis usually raises potassium
Assess and urgently arrange verification with the team
Remove the result from the handover because it is haemolysed
Treat the value as definitive without noting haemolysis
why: A possible artefact does not exclude dangerous true hyperkalaemia.
Haemolysis may distort potassium, but true elevation must be excluded.
The result and specimen-quality issue both need timely communication and verification.
Sample quality may alter treatment decisions.
proposedChanges.stem: A stable adult has potassium 6.7 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0) in a sample labelled significantly haemolysed. Which action is most appropriate?

items.assessment: Mild postoperative white-cell elevation alone does not diagnose infection; trend and full assessment are appropriate. The key avoids both antibiotic reflex and an absolute fever rule.
Target-based INR interpretation is correct; pulse-only effectiveness assessment is an unrelated distractor.
issues: Target-based INR interpretation is correct; pulse-only effectiveness assessment is an unrelated distractor.

options: Compare only with the laboratory's healthy-person range
Assume every elevated INR indicates active haemorrhage
Compare with the previous INR only, without checking the current prescribed target
Compare it with that target and bleeding findings
why: The intended therapeutic range differs from untreated values.
An elevated result indicates risk, not proof of bleeding.
A previous value may also be outside target; compare with the current therapeutic plan and clinical bleeding findings.
The individual target and symptoms guide escalation.

items.assessment: Two options are the same dietary-history delay, weakening discrimination.
issues: Two options are the same dietary-history delay, weakening discrimination.

options: Test leg strength in detail before checking the pulse and rhythm
Assess oral intake and gastric losses before obtaining current cardiac findings
Cardiac rate and rhythm with escalation
Repeat assessment of bowel motility
why: Confirming the weakness does not take priority over the potential cardiac conduction complication.
Loss history matters, but cardiac assessment should not be postponed in this symptomatic low-potassium case.
Potassium depletion can disturb cardiac conduction.
Ileus can accompany depletion, but cardiac conduction effects take priority.

items.assessment: Albumin affected by inflammation/fluid state should not be used alone to diagnose malnutrition. Broader assessment is the only defensible interpretation; ASPEN explicitly supports the limitation. Foundation/application boundary is acceptable.
Recollection after contaminated sampling is correct; isolation based only on mixed flora is not a plausible competing choice.
issues: Recollection after contaminated sampling is correct; isolation based only on mixed flora is not a plausible competing choice.

options: Discuss recollection using the ordered clean method
Assume several simultaneous infections
Use whichever organism has the highest colony count without reviewing collection quality
Discard symptoms because the sample is poor
why: Contamination limits interpretation of the original sample.
Mixed organisms can reflect collection contamination.
A mixed contaminated specimen may not support reliable organism-specific interpretation; clinical context and recollection matter.
Symptoms still require assessment despite an unreliable specimen.

items.assessment: Laboratory-guided restart is correct, but adding water is an implausible specimen substitution.
issues: Laboratory-guided restart is correct, but adding water is an implausible specimen substitution.

options: Collect the next void separately and add it after the planned 24-hour endpoint
Extend collection by an arbitrary hour
Send the collection without noting the omission
Notify the laboratory and follow restart instructions
why: An extra later void does not reliably replace analytes from a missed interval; obtain laboratory guidance.
An extra hour does not reliably replace the missed sample.
The laboratory needs the limitation to interpret validity.
An incomplete timed sample may invalidate the result.

items.assessment: Toilet urine and a used jug are glaring contamination errors; use more realistic clean-catch misconceptions.
issues: Toilet urine and a used jug are glaring contamination errors; use more realistic clean-catch misconceptions.

options: Catch the first urine immediately to avoid losing organisms from the sample
Rest the open lid inner-surface down on the bedside table while collecting
Begin voiding before collecting the sample
Avoid touching the inside of the container
why: The requested midstream sample begins after initial voiding.
Contact with the surface can contaminate the lid and specimen container.
Midstream collection reduces contamination from initial urethral washout.
Contact can introduce organisms into the specimen.

items.assessment: Deep cough/recollection is correct; adding water to a culture is a cartoon action.
issues: Deep cough/recollection is correct; adding water to a culture is a cartoon action.

options: Collect immediately after mouthwash without checking instructions
Coach a deep cough and recollect as ordered
Send it as adequate because volume is sufficient
Pool several saliva samples until the requested volume is reached
why: Some collection preparations may affect specimen quality.
A lower-respiratory sample is needed for the requested test.
Volume does not establish respiratory specimen quality.
Increasing saliva volume does not turn it into a lower-respiratory specimen.

items.assessment: Method-specific instructions are useful, but a container from last year is implausible.
issues: Method-specific instructions are useful, but a container from last year is implausible.

options: Follow the current kit's specific instructions
Apply every restriction from the old kit
Collect during visible rectal bleeding without checking guidance
Transfer a specimen into a standard urine container because all stool tests use the same preservative
why: Collection and dietary requirements vary by test method.
Unneeded restrictions can confuse or impair completion.
Active bleeding may affect interpretation and requires appropriate advice.
Collection device and preservative depend on the specific stool test; follow its current instructions.

items.assessment: Cultures before promptly available antibiotics is correct; cancelling because fever falls is simplistic.
issues: Cultures before promptly available antibiotics is correct; cancelling because fever falls is simplistic.

options: Wait for the next fever peak
Start the antibiotic and collect cultures at the next routine phlebotomy visit
Delay antibiotics until preliminary culture results are available
Collect cultures before antibiotics without delaying urgent care
why: Waiting can delay needed antimicrobial treatment.
When collection is promptly possible without treatment delay, pretreatment sampling improves yield.
Cultures should not delay urgent antimicrobial treatment while results are awaited.
Pre-treatment sampling improves yield while preserving timely treatment.

items.assessment: Identity resolution is correct, but asking whether a lab value feels familiar is unrelated filler.
issues: Identity resolution is correct, but asking whether a lab value feels familiar is unrelated filler.

options: Copy it into the chart and clarify later
Ask the sending unit to confirm the name alone before accepting the result
Resolve the identification discrepancy
Accept it because names match

One matching identifier does not resolve the conflicting date of birth.
Treatment requires confirmation that the result belongs to this client.

items.assessment: Named responsibility/contact is sound; next-year follow-up is implausibly delayed.
issues: Named responsibility/contact is sound; next-year follow-up is implausibly delayed.

items.assessment: Storage-specific review is correct; a larger container cannot plausibly correct delay.
issues: Storage-specific review is correct; a larger container cannot plausibly correct delay.

Send it later without noting the delay
Freeze it without laboratory guidance
Refrigerate the sample now and omit documenting how long it remained at room temperature
why: Delay can alter results and may require recollection.

Unapproved storage can damage specimen integrity.
Later cooling does not undo the delay; the laboratory needs the time/storage history.

items.assessment: Trend plus clinical context is correct; explicitly unrelated history is an obvious negative.
issues: Trend plus clinical context is correct; explicitly unrelated history is an obvious negative.

options: Current symptoms and relevant treatment
Only that the computer highlighted the number

why: Clinical context helps establish urgency and likely causes.
A flag alone omits essential clinical information.
